title: How to look up a function in Numbers on Mac with Formulas and Functions Help
metaTitle: Look Up a Function in Numbers on Mac, Step by Step
description: Learn how to look up a function in Numbers on Mac using the Help menu and the Functions Browser, with steps for Numbers 15.4 and error fixes.

Formulas and Functions Help Numbers Mac
intro: To look up a function in Numbers on Mac, open Numbers, click Help in the menu bar, and choose Formulas and Functions Help. To find one inside a spreadsheet, type an equal sign in a cell, then search the Functions Browser and double-click the function you want.
tldr: Open Numbers, then choose Help > Formulas and Functions Help from the menu bar.
To look up a function inside a cell, type = in the cell, then search the Functions Browser.
Double-click a function to place it in the Formula Editor with its arguments.
Click the red triangle in an error cell to read the message, fix the reference, then press Return.
The Apple guide covers Numbers 15.4, which needs macOS 26 or later.

blocks.text: Apple keeps the function reference inside Numbers, so you do not need a web search to learn what a function does. The Help menu opens Formulas and Functions Help. The Functions Browser lists every function while you build a formula. The Numbers User Guide for Mac says it covers Numbers 15.4, so check your version first.
Open Formulas and Functions Help from the Help menu

Click Help in the menu bar at the top of the screen. Then choose Formulas and Functions Help. Apple's page explains how to use formulas and functions in your spreadsheet. It also covers the argument types, condition types, and wildcards that formulas accept.
Read the condition and wildcard sections before you guess at a format. A function that counts or matches values often needs its condition written in a specific way.
Check how many functions the guide lists

Apple's heading on that page says Explore more than 300 functions. The iCloud guide for Numbers says more than 250 built-in functions. Apple's web guide says hundreds. Those figures conflict, and the pages checked do not say which one is current.
Treat the total as a rough guide. What matters more is that the browser lists each function with its arguments. You do not need to memorize the count.
Search the guide on the web version
Apple's web version of Formulas and Functions Help has a Table of Contents link at the top of the page. It also has a Search this guide field. Those controls are documented for the web guide.

The Mac Help window may show the same controls, but this guide could not confirm that. If you do not see a search field, use the Table of Contents or your browser's find feature. Apple lists COT among the functions added in Numbers 15.4, so it is a good test. If COT is missing from your Functions Browser, your version may be older.
Look up a function from inside a cell
Most people look up a function while they type a formula. Click an empty cell, then type an equal sign (=). The Formula Editor opens over the cell.

The Functions Browser appears on the right side of the window and lists all functions. Apple's iCloud guide places the browser in the sidebar instead. Look for a list of functions and a search field, wherever your window shows them.
Find the function in the Functions Browser
Click the search field at the top of the Functions Browser. Type a function name or a related term. Apple's example is the word address. Searching by task works when you do not know the exact name.

Here is a worked example. Say you need the cotangent of a value. Type COT in the search field, and the list narrows. Double-click COT. It lands in the Formula Editor with its arguments, ready for values.
Insert a function from the toolbar instead
You do not have to start in a cell. Click the Insert button in the toolbar, then choose New Formula. This opens the Formula Editor and the Functions Browser, just like typing an equal sign.
This route helps when you want to browse functions before you commit to a cell. It is also the quickest route if you are not sure where the result should go.
Read the arguments and fill them in

Double-clicking a function puts it in the Formula Editor with its required and optional arguments. Required arguments must get a value. Optional arguments can stay empty, or you can add them when you need them.
Apple's notes list three keys that matter here. Command-K preserves both the row and column of a selected range. Delete removes selected cell references. Return commits the formula.

items: Command-K: preserve both the row and column of a selected range
Commit Formula button: finishes the formula, the same as Return

blocks.text: Apple lists no Option, Control, or Shift shortcuts for the Formula Editor. Do not spend time searching for them.
Read the error triangles in a result cell

A formula error shows a red triangle in the middle of the result cell. A blue triangle in the upper left means one or more warnings. Click either icon to open a message window that summarizes each error and warning.
If the message points to another cell, click that cell reference in the message to select it. Then you can see which input caused the problem. Read the message before you change anything.
Fix a broken formula and commit it again
Double-click the result cell. The Formula Editor reopens with your formula. Change, remove, or add references as needed.
Press Return or click the Commit Formula button. Check the result cell. If the red triangle stays, click the icon again and read the new message.
Common causes of formula errors in Numbers
Apple lists six common causes. Check these before you rebuild the formula from scratch.

items: Typos or invalid cell references in the formula
Self-reference, where a formula refers to its own cell
Text that is not in double quotation marks
Numbers stored as text, fixed by setting a numeric format in the inspector
A deleted cell that the formula still refers to
References that shifted after you inserted a row or column

blocks.text: Text is the sneaky one. A number that looks right can fail if Numbers stores it as text. Select the cell, open the inspector, and set a numeric format.
This guide found no Apple-documented fix for #NAME? errors. The Apple pages checked do not cover that message, so this guide does not give one.
Which Numbers version adds the newer functions
Numbers 15.4 requires macOS 26 or later. It adds 18 functions, including trigonometry, statistics, and logic functions. Examples include COT, GAMMA, PEARSON, XOR, and DAYS.
Numbers 14.4 added over 30 functions earlier. Those include LET, LAMBDA, FILTER, SORT, and UNIQUE. It also added spilling arrays, so one formula result can fill several cells.
To check your version, open Numbers > About Numbers. If your version is older than 15.4, the newest functions may not appear in the browser. Match your version to the guide before you troubleshoot.
What Apple Creator Studio changed in Numbers 15.1
Numbers 15.1 became part of Apple Creator Studio. Apple says creating, viewing, editing, and real-time collaboration do not need a subscription. Content Hub and generative AI image tools do.
The subscription details do not change the Help menu or the Functions Browser, as far as Apple's pages describe.
Mistakes people make when they look up a function

items: Skipping the equal sign. Without it, you have typed text, not a formula.
Ignoring the argument names. They show what each input expects.
Typing a text value without double quotation marks around it.
Trusting results after inserting a row or column. Apple lists shifted references as a cause of errors.
Assuming every Apple page shows the same function count or the same browser layout.
Clicking the red triangle, reading nothing, and deleting the formula.

blocks.text: Keyboard shortcuts in the Formula Editor
Return does most of the work. It commits the formula, and it is usually the last key you press. Command-K and Delete help you select and change references.
The Apple pages checked do not list a keyboard shortcut for opening Formulas and Functions Help or the Functions Browser. Use the Help menu and the toolbar for those.
Next steps after you find the function
Once the formula works, you may want to sort the rows that feed it. The guide on [how to sort a table in Numbers on Mac by column](/how-to/sort-a-table-by-column-in-numbers) walks through that step.
For more on Numbers features, see the [Numbers page for Mac](/apps/numbers). Use Apple's guide as the final check when a function behaves differently from what you read here.

faq.question: Where is Formulas and Functions Help in Numbers on Mac?
faq.answer: Click Help in the menu bar, then choose Formulas and Functions Help. Apple's steps say to open Numbers first, then use that menu. The guide covers Numbers 15.4, so check your version in Numbers > About Numbers.

faq.question: How do I look up a function without leaving my spreadsheet?
faq.answer: Click an empty cell and type an equal sign. The Formula Editor opens, and the Functions Browser lists every function. Type a name in its search field and double-click the one you want.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut for Formulas and Functions Help?
faq.answer: Not in the Apple pages checked. Use the Help menu. Inside the Formula Editor, Return commits the formula and Command-K preserves a range's row and column.

faq.question: How many functions does Numbers have?
faq.answer: Apple gives different answers. Its guide heading says more than 300, the iCloud guide says more than 250 built-in functions, and the web guide says hundreds. Use the browser list as the working reference.

faq.question: What does the red triangle in my cell mean?
faq.answer: It means a formula error. Click the icon to read the message. If the message points to a cell, click that reference to select it, then double-click the result cell to fix the formula.

faq.question: What does a blue triangle mean?
faq.answer: Apple says a blue triangle in the upper left means one or more warnings. Click it to read the message window, then decide whether the warning needs any action.

faq.question: Which Numbers version do I need for the newest functions?
faq.answer: Numbers 15.4 requires macOS 26 or later. It adds 18 functions, such as COT and XOR. Check your version in Numbers > About Numbers before you assume a function is missing.

faq.question: Does the Functions Browser work on iPhone and iCloud too?
faq.answer: Apple's web guide says the Functions Browser is available in Numbers on Mac or iCloud.com, and in Numbers on iPhone or iPad. The Mac page and the iCloud page place it differently, so check your own window.

steps.name: Open Numbers and the Help menu
steps.text: Open Numbers on your Mac, then click Help in the menu bar at the top of the screen.
steps.tip: Numbers > About Numbers shows your version. The Apple guide covers Numbers 15.4.

steps.name: Choose Formulas and Functions Help
steps.text: Choose Formulas and Functions Help from the Help menu. Apple's guide explains formulas, functions, argument types, condition types, and wildcards.
steps.tip: On the web version, use the Table of Contents link or the Search this guide field at the top.

steps.name: Pick an empty cell
steps.text: Open a spreadsheet and click an empty cell in a table. Formulas go in cells, so choose the cell where you want the result.
steps.tip: Choose a cell outside your data so you do not overwrite a value by accident.

steps.name: Type an equal sign
steps.text: Type an equal sign (=) in the cell. The Formula Editor opens over the cell, and the Functions Browser lists all functions.
steps.tip: Apple's iCloud guide places the browser in the sidebar. Check where it shows on your screen.

steps.name: Or use the Insert button
steps.text: Click the Insert button in the toolbar and choose New Formula. This opens the Formula Editor and the Functions Browser without typing in a cell first.
steps.tip: Use this route when you want to browse functions before you pick a cell.

steps.name: Search the Functions Browser
steps.text: Click the search field at the top of the Functions Browser. Type a function name, such as COT, or a related term, such as address.
steps.tip: If you do not know the name, search by the task you want to do.

steps.name: Double-click the function
steps.text: Double-click the function in the list. It appears in the Formula Editor with its required and optional arguments.
steps.tip: Read each argument name before you type a value into it.

steps.name: Fill in the arguments
steps.text: Click a cell to add its reference, or type a value. Press Command-K to preserve both the row and column of a selected range. Press Delete to remove selected cell references.
steps.tip: Put text values in double quotation marks, or the formula reports an error.

steps.name: Commit the formula
steps.text: Press Return or click the Commit Formula button. The result appears in the cell.
steps.tip: Commit Formula is the button in the Formula Editor. It does the same job as Return.

steps.name: Read an error icon
steps.text: If a formula fails, a Syntax Error icon appears in the result cell. It is a red triangle in the middle of the cell. Click it to read the message.
steps.tip: If the message points to another cell, click that reference to select it.

steps.name: Fix the formula and commit again
steps.text: Double-click the result cell to reopen the Formula Editor. Change, remove, or add references. Press Return or click Commit Formula.
steps.tip: Check the result cell again. If the red triangle stays, read the new message.

troubleshooting.problem: The Functions Browser is not where Apple's guide says
troubleshooting.fix: Apple's Mac page says the browser sits on the right side, and the iCloud page says the sidebar. Look at your window and widen it if the browser is cut off. This guide could not check a live Numbers 15.4 layout, so trust what you see.

troubleshooting.problem: A red triangle appears in a formula cell
troubleshooting.fix: Click the icon to read the message. If the message names a cell, click that reference. Double-click the result cell, fix the reference, and press Return.

troubleshooting.problem: A blue triangle appears in the upper left of a cell
troubleshooting.fix: A blue triangle means one or more warnings, not an error. Click it, read the message window, and decide whether the warning needs action.

troubleshooting.problem: A formula with correct-looking numbers returns an error
troubleshooting.fix: The numbers may be stored as text. Select the cell, open the inspector, and set a numeric format. Then commit the formula again.

troubleshooting.problem: A formula broke after you inserted a row or column
troubleshooting.fix: Apple lists shifted references as a cause. Double-click the result cell and check each reference against the table as it looks now.

troubleshooting.problem: The newest functions are missing from the browser
troubleshooting.fix: Functions such as COT came with Numbers 15.4, which needs macOS 26 or later. Check Numbers > About Numbers, then update if your Mac supports it.
